clue.text: Regret Bob ill — upset for nouveau romancier

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the preceding words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone regrets that Bob is unwell, before a French novelist is mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges REGRET, BOB and ILL into the French writer's hyphenated surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Alain Robbe-Grillet was the leading practitioner of the French experimental novel of the 1950s, the nouveau roman.

clue.text: Fast mover exemplified by Mr Toad (hopping over the species barrier)

definitions.text: Fast mover exemplified by Mr Toad (hopping over the species barrier)

parts.words: Fast mover exemplified by Mr Toad (hopping over the species barrier)
parts.note: Mr Toad of The Wind in the Willows is a reckless motorist; turn his amphibian into a farm animal and you get a term for a selfish speeding driver

explanation.surface: Kenneth Grahame's Toad roars off in his motor car, the very image of a road menace.
explanation.walkthrough: Toad is the archetypal careless driver; swap the toad for a pig (the species barrier) to get the term for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A selfish, aggressive motorist who dominates the highway is called by this porcine compound.

clue.text: A single man in possession of a good fortune"

definitions.text: A single man in possession of a good fortune"

parts.words: A single man in possession of a good fortune"
parts.note: the famous opening sentence of Pride and Prejudice, which Mrs Bennet applies to the wealthy newcomer at Netherfield

explanation.surface: A quotation from Jane Austen's opening line about wealthy bachelors.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is the opening of Pride and Prejudice; the single man in question is the new tenant of Netherfield Park.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Bingley is the rich unmarried gentleman whose arrival at Netherfield sets Austen's novel going.

clue.text: Like all Yeats's other lovers (if not dead)

definitions.text: Like all Yeats's other lovers (if not dead)

parts.words: Like all Yeats's other lovers (if not dead)
parts.note: the poet's past loves, unless they have died, are now distant from him and parted from his affections

explanation.surface: A remark about the fate of the women W. B. Yeats once loved.
explanation.walkthrough: Former lovers who are still alive are, by implication, alienated or parted from the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone alienated or separated from a former partner is described with this word.

clue.text: J.C. Harris's avuncular narrator

parts.note: Joel Chandler Harris's folk tales are told by an elderly man known by the title Uncle

explanation.surface: A reference to the storyteller in Joel Chandler Harris's tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avuncular' points to the title Uncle borne by the narrator of the Brer Rabbit stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Remus is the old storyteller who narrates Joel Chandler Harris's Brer Rabbit tales.

clue.text: "(She) cried through the, Why is his chariot so long in coming 7" (Judges)

definitions.text: "(She) cried through the, Why is his chariot so long in coming 7" (Judges)

parts.words: "(She) cried through the, Why is his chariot so long in coming 7" (Judges)
parts.note: a quotation from the Song of Deborah, Judges 5:28, with a gap for the window screen through which Sisera's mother looks out

explanation.surface: A biblical quotation with a missing word about a mother waiting for her son.
explanation.walkthrough: Judges 5:28 reads 'The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice'; the '7' is the page's question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the crisscross screen of a window in the King James text.

clue.text: To gripe, perhaps, at journey undertaken by 1?

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters of the words before it are only one possible arrangement, so they are shuffled

explanation.surface: Grumbling about a trip taken by the novelist at 1 across.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges TO GRIPE; '1' is read as I, the self, so the journey is one taken by the ego.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-indulgent venture undertaken purely for vanity is called this, the 1 standing for I, the self.

clue.text: Play with lady army officer

parts.note: a major is a rank of army officer

explanation.surface: A drama featuring a woman serving as an officer in the army.
explanation.walkthrough: The charade is taken in answer order: the rank before the name, as in Shaw's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Major Barbara is George Bernard Shaw's 1905 drama about a Salvation Army officer.

clue.text: Is Huysmans's attitude to character opposed?

definitions.meaning: Huysmans's novel A rebours is known in English as ... Nature, and nature here is character

explanation.surface: A question about whether the French decadent Huysmans was hostile to character.
explanation.definitionFit: The preposition means contrary or hostile, and it begins the English title of Huysmans's novel about nature.

clue.text: English recorder of French lives with German car

parts.note: mit is the German word for with
a Ford is a make of car

explanation.surface: An English biographer of French figures teams up with a German motor.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy Mitford wrote lives of Madame de Pompadour, Voltaire and Louis XIV.
explanation.definitionFit: Nancy Mitford, an English novelist, wrote biographies of Pompadour, Voltaire and the Sun King.

clue.text: Stormy story of ghostly apparition

definitions.meaning: Theodor Storm wrote the novella Ein ..., so it is a story by Storm
a spectral double of a living person

explanation.surface: A tale told on a wild night about a phantom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stormy' means by Theodor Storm, the German novelist, not tempestuous.
explanation.definitionFit: In German folklore, a person's spectral twin is seen as an omen; Storm's 1887 novella bears the same title.

clue.text: Her brother was urged to be true to himself

definitions.text: Her brother was urged to be true to himself

parts.words: Her brother was urged to be true to himself
parts.note: Polonius tells his son Laertes 'to thine own self be true'; the clue points to Laertes's sister

explanation.surface: A remark about a young man given advice about sincerity, through his sister.
explanation.walkthrough: Polonius's advice in Hamlet is given to Laertes; the clue asks for his sister.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophelia, daughter of Polonius in Hamlet, is the sister of Laertes.

clue.text: "Idle to hope that the simple - -pump/ Can extinguish hell" (Henry Reed)

definitions.text: "Idle to hope that the simple - -pump/ Can extinguish hell" (Henry Reed)

parts.words: "Idle to hope that the simple - -pump/ Can extinguish hell" (Henry Reed)
parts.note: a line from Henry Reed's wartime verse with a gap before the hand pump used against incendiary bombs

explanation.surface: A quotation from Henry Reed about the futility of firefighting in the Blitz.
explanation.walkthrough: The stirrup-pump was a small hand pump issued in Britain in the Second World War to tackle incendiary fires.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word completes the name of the wartime hand-operated fire pump, steadied by a foot loop.

clue.text: The colonel is not quite up to par

definitions.meaning: Colonel ..., the march and the imaginary golf opponent
in golf, a score of one stroke over the standard for a hole

explanation.surface: A remark that the colonel is a little off-colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonel Bogey is the famous march; in golf the word means a hole played in one stroke more than standard.

clue.text: Kipling described his fall in What Fothergill Espied

indicators.note: in signals that the letters are found inside the following words, running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A mock title for a Kipling piece about something Fothergill saw.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden run spans the end of 'Fothergill' and the start of 'Espied'.
explanation.definitionFit: General Rollo Gillespie was killed storming the fort at Kalunga in 1814, a death commemorated in verse by Kipling.

clue.text: Droll love tangle of ballad hero

indicators.note: a tangle is a muddle, so the letters of the words before it are knotted into a new order

explanation.surface: An amusing romantic mix-up involving the hero of a ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tangle' rearranges DROLL and LOVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Lovel is the hero of a traditional English folk ballad who returns to find his love dead.

clue.text: Rest of unreadable book

definitions.meaning: a book that no one would read is sold off cheaply as unsold stock

explanation.surface: Something left of a dull volume.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means what is left; publishers also apply it to unsold copies dumped at a reduced price.

clue.text: "Ex cathedra" lady in Lonsdale piece

annotationWithheld.why: "Ex cathedra" lady in Lonsdale piece (7): no parse found giving the answer; the Lonsdale reference and the role of 'lady' could not be identified, and searches of the clue text found nothing

clue.text: Stressful, yet camp way of life, as reported in old war books

indicators.note: as reported means the words are heard rather than read, so a phrase that sounds the same is wanted

parts.note: living under canvas, in tents, is the way of life in a camp

explanation.surface: Life in camp described as stressful in old war books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as reported' gives the sound of IN TENTS. 'camp' wants to be the theatrical sense; it is the military camp of old war books.
explanation.definitionFit: Highly strained or strongly felt, as is a nerve-racking situation.

clue.text: Novelist warned us to Read All About It

definitions.text: Novelist warned us to Read All About It

parts.words: Novelist warned us to Read All About It
parts.note: Read All About It was a BBC books programme presented by the Cumbrian novelist Melvyn

explanation.surface: A writer urging the public to read the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read All About It' is the title of the 1970s BBC books programme presented by Melvyn Bragg, not a newspaper-seller's cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Melvyn Bragg, novelist and broadcaster, fronted the BBC books programme of that name.

clue.text: What moonbeam does at sea, according to the Ancient Mariner

definitions.text: What moonbeam does at sea, according to the Ancient Mariner

parts.words: What moonbeam does at sea, according to the Ancient Mariner
parts.note: Coleridge writes that the moon's beams mocked the sultry main, using an archaic intensified verb

explanation.surface: A question about moonlight on the ocean in Coleridge's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge: 'Her beams bemocked the sultry main, / Like April hoar-frost spread.'
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's verb means derides or makes a mockery of, used of moonlight on the sea.

clue.text: Diana merits a whole new look

indicators.note: a whole new look means the preceding letters are given a complete makeover into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Diana deserves a fresh image, as a fashion makeover might promise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'whole new look' rearranges MERITS A into the Greek goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess of the hunt was identified with her Greek counterpart.

clue.text: Ten neat arrangements for a Gothic maid, so to speak

indicators.note: arrangements means the letters of the words before it are set out in a different order

explanation.surface: Various tidy orderings of ten things for a maid in a Gothic novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangements' rearranges TEN NEAT. Annette is the chattering maid in Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho.
explanation.definitionFit: Annette is Emily's talkative servant in Radcliffe's Gothic novel The Mysteries of Udolpho.

clue.text: Record to choose for Eleusinian initiate

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: Picking a recording for someone joining the ancient Greek mysteries.
explanation.walkthrough: An epopt was one admitted to the highest grade of the Eleusinian Mysteries in ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greek religion, one admitted to the highest secrets of the Mysteries at Eleusis.

clue.text: Joe in the attic?

parts.note: the attic is the room at the top of a house, pointing to John Braine's novel Room at the Top and its hero Joe

explanation.surface: A man named Joe up in the loft.
explanation.walkthrough: The attic is the room at the top, the title of John Braine's 1957 novel whose ambitious hero is Joe.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Lampton is the social-climbing protagonist of John Braine's novel Room at the Top.

clue.text: Shakespearean sea captain, relegated by Gilbert to gondolier

definitions.meaning: the mariner who rescues Sebastian in Twelfth Night
in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers the same name is borne by a mere boatman

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean seaman demoted by W. S. Gilbert to a Venetian boatman.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio is the captain who befriends Sebastian in Twelfth Night, and a minor boatman in The Gondoliers.

clue.text: A nobleman of parts from Bragelonne

definitions.text: A nobleman of parts from Bragelonne

parts.words: A nobleman of parts from Bragelonne
parts.note: Dumas's long novel about a titled Frenchman from Bragelonne is published in several parts

explanation.surface: A talented aristocrat hailing from Bragelonne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of parts' suggests talent, but it means the book is issued in parts: Dumas's Le Vicomte de Bragelonne is so long that English editions split it.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Vicomte de Bragelonne is Dumas's Musketeer novel; the French title is a noble rank below count.

clue.text: Terrible sin Aristotle ascribed to students of Chinese

indicators.note: terrible here means badly mangled, so the letters of the words after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dreadful sin attributed by Aristotle to scholars of China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' rearranges SIN ARISTOTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Scholars of Eastern languages and cultures, such as sinologists, were traditionally given this name.
